1366.title: Om mani padme hum
1366.hook: six syllables, spun in prayer wheels and carved into stones along mountain paths
1366.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists often recite om mani padme hum on prayer beads, turn prayer wheels that contain it, and carve or print it on stones and flags, as an expression of the compassion of Chenrezig.

segments.voice: Yesterday, lamrim, the staircase of the path, starting from a precious human life. Your line was precious human life. Today, a sound Tibetan Buddhists send out into the world.

A brass cylinder the size of a coffee can, set on a handle. An older woman walks around a temple, turning it with a flick of the wrist, clockwise, again and again, her lips moving. Along the path outside, flat stones are stacked into walls, each carved with the same row of letters. Up on the ridge, prayer flags carry them too. Inside the cylinder, tightly rolled, is paper printed over and over with those letters. The whole landscape seems to be saying one sentence: six syllables that Tibetan Buddhists tie to compassion.
screen: `A WHEEL TURNED CLOCKWISE.` → `STONES CARVED ALONG THE PATH.` → `ONE SENTENCE, EVERYWHERE.`

segments.voice: Om mani padme hum is a mantra, a sacred sound to be repeated, the kind of word you met back on day one hundred two. First, whose sound it is. Tibetan Buddhists connect it with Avalokiteshvara, called Chenrezig in Tibetan, the bodhisattva of compassion, the one who hears the cries of the world. A Mahayana scripture, the Karandavyuha Sutra, praises it at length. To say it is to turn the mind toward that compassion. Second, the words. Mani is a jewel; padma is a lotus. So a common English rendering is your line: the jewel in the lotus. That's a start, not a settled one. Scholars argue over the grammar, and Tibetan teachers often skip the translation and explain the syllables one at a time, each linked to a quality to cultivate or a kind of suffering to be freed from. Third, the wheel and the stone. Written inside a prayer wheel, the mantra is said to be sent out with every turn. Carved on a stone, it stays there for every passerby. Printed on a flag, the wind carries it. Compassion shouldn't depend on one person remembering to say it. Fourth, the picture. The lotus grows up out of mud and opens clean, an image teachers use for a mind that stays open in a messy world. The jewel is something precious that was there all along. You don't need to settle the grammar to hold both pictures.
screen: `THE SOUND OF COMPASSION.` · `JEWEL, LOTUS, AND A GRAMMAR DEBATE.` · `SPUN, CARVED, CARRIED BY WIND.` · `A LOTUS OUT OF MUD.`

segments.voice: If you'd like, say the mantra softly, om mani padme hum, at an easy, steady pace, the way it's said in Tibetan homes and temples. If saying it doesn't fit you, listen to it inwardly, or rest with the breath and the picture of a lotus opening above muddy water. There's nothing to achieve; let the sound, or the quiet, do the work.
Om mani padme hum. The mantra of compassion in Tibetan Buddhism, linked to Chenrezig, spun in wheels and carved in stone. Often rendered the jewel in the lotus. Today's word.
Your line: the jewel in the lotus. Something precious, open in the mud. Until tomorrow.

1367.title: The teacher and lineage
1367.hook: a Tibetan teacher reads a text aloud to students who could read it themselves, and that's the point
1367.howItsDone: In Tibetan Buddhism, students receive a practice from a teacher through a reading transmission, an empowerment and instructions, and lineages recite prayers naming the teachers who passed it down.

segments.voice: Yesterday, om mani padme hum, spun in wheels and carved in stone. Your line was the jewel in the lotus. Today, how a practice like that gets handed on.

A room full of students, each with a copy of the text. Every one of them can read. And yet a teacher at the front reads the whole thing aloud, quickly, sometimes so fast it's hard to follow, from the first line to the last. Nobody takes notes. Nobody asks questions. From the back of the room it can look like a strange use of an afternoon. But in Tibetan Buddhism, something is being handed over that isn't on the page: permission, connection, a living link back through the people who read it to the people who read it to this teacher.
screen: `EVERYONE HAS THE TEXT.` → `THE TEACHER READS IT ALOUD.` → `SOMETHING NOT ON THE PAGE.`

segments.voice: Back on day one thousand three hundred fifty-seven, Zen showed us the teacher face to face. Tibetan Buddhism puts the teacher at the center too, in its own shape. First, the teacher. In Tibetan the word is lama, used for the Sanskrit guru. Tibetan texts treat the teacher as the doorway to practice, the one who makes the teaching alive for a particular student. Second, the reading. What happened in that room is called a lung, a reading transmission: the text read aloud so it's received by ear from someone who received it the same way. Third, empowerment. Some Tibetan practices, especially visualizing a buddha or reciting certain mantras, are begun only after an empowerment, a ceremony in which a qualified teacher introduces the student to that practice. Some texts and practices stay closed until then. Not secret for the sake of it, the tradition says, but because without guidance they can be misunderstood. Fourth, the lineage. Each practice is said to come down an unbroken chain, teacher to student, and lineages have prayers that name the chain one person at a time. Practicing means stepping into that line. And the tradition keeps a balance: Tibetan texts on finding a teacher warn the student to examine a teacher carefully, sometimes for a long time, before trusting them. Respect and care belong together. Some things can be learned from a book. Some can't.
screen: `THE LAMA, THE DOORWAY.` · `THE READING: RECEIVED BY EAR.` · `EMPOWERMENT BEFORE PRACTICE.` · `A CHAIN OF PEOPLE, AND CARE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you've been trying to learn alone, from books or videos: an instrument, a language, a way of prayer or meditation. Where does it keep stalling? Then ask the question the Tibetan texts ask: if a guide were to help with this, what would you want to see in them before trusting them, patience, honesty, their own practice? Don't decide anything; let the question sit.
The teacher and lineage. In Tibetan Buddhism, the lama who gives the reading and the empowerment, and the chain of teachers behind them. Today's word.
Your line: some things need a teacher. And a teacher is worth examining before you trust one. Go gently.

1368.title: The sand mandala
1368.hook: monks build a palace of colored sand grain by grain, and then sweep it into a jar
1368.howItsDone: Tibetan monks make sand mandalas for particular ceremonies, working with chanting and fine metal funnels, and when the ceremony ends they dismantle the mandala with prayers, sharing some sand and pouring the rest into flowing water.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the teacher and lineage: the reading aloud, the empowerment, the chain of people. Your line was some things need a teacher. Today, something monks make together, and then unmake.

A low square table in a museum lobby. Around it, a few Tibetan monks lean in so close their noses nearly touch the surface. Each holds a thin metal funnel and rubs a rod along its ridged side, and the vibration lets out colored sand, a few grains at a time. A thin blue line. A red petal. A gold edge. Visitors come back day after day to watch the circle grow, more detailed than seems possible. Then, at the end, the monks chant, pick up brushes, and sweep the whole thing from the edges into the center. A gray-brown pile. A jar.
screen: `A FUNNEL. A FEW GRAINS.` → `THE CIRCLE GROWS.` → `THEN THE BRUSHES COME OUT.`

segments.voice: Mandala is a Sanskrit word for a circle. In Tibetan Buddhism a mandala is a picture of an awakened world, often drawn as a palace seen from above, with a buddha or deity at the center and gates opening in each direction. First, it's a map, not a decoration. Every color, symbol and line has a meaning in the practice it belongs to. A sand mandala is usually made for a particular ceremony, and those who use it in practice learn to visualize the palace in their minds. Second, the making is itself practice. The monks work with chanting and concentration, grain by grain. A shaky hand or a sneeze can undo an hour. Patience isn't a side effect; it's part of the offering. Third, the sweep. When the ceremony is done, the mandala is dismantled on purpose, with prayers. Some of the sand is given to people watching as a blessing, and the rest is often carried to a river or other flowing water and poured in, so the blessing travels on. Fourth, why sweep it at all? Buddhist teaching holds that everything made of parts comes apart: impermanence. The sweep makes that teaching visible. All that skill, all that beauty, and the hand that made it is the hand that clears it away. For some watching, the sweep doesn't look like a loss. It looks like the last step of the work.
screen: `A PALACE SEEN FROM ABOVE.` · `THE MAKING IS PRACTICE.` · `SWEPT UP, POURED INTO WATER.` · `EVERYTHING MADE COMES APART.`

segments.voice: Gather a few small things within reach, coins, pens, keys, a leaf, a cup, and slowly arrange them into a small pattern with a center, taking care with each one. Then, with the same care, gather it all back up, one piece at a time, and put each thing where it came from. Notice what the letting go feels like in your hands.
The sand mandala. A Tibetan picture of an awakened world, built grain by grain for a ceremony, and then swept away to show that everything made comes apart. Today's word.
Your line: sweep it away. Even something beautiful is allowed to end. That's today, done.

1369.title: The desert
1369.hook: a monk in an Egyptian cell keeps checking the window to see if the sun has moved
1369.howItsDone: In Orthodox and Catholic monastic life, Evagrius and the desert fathers and mothers are read for guidance on prayer, and some Christians practice noticing and naming troubling thoughts as part of their prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sand mandala, built grain by grain and swept into a jar. Your line was sweep it away. That closes our time with Tibetan Buddhism. Today a new stretch begins: Christian contemplative ways, starting in the desert.

Late morning in a small stone cell in the Egyptian desert. A monk is supposed to be praying and reading. Instead he gets up and looks out the door to see whether the sun has moved. It hasn't, much. He sits back down. A minute later he's up again, checking whether anyone is coming to visit. He starts to think the other monks don't care about him, that he'd be holier somewhere else, anywhere else. A monk named Evagrius wrote this scene down, almost like a field guide entry, and gave the restless thing a name. He wasn't writing to shame the monk. He was mapping the terrain.
screen: `A CELL IN THE DESERT.` → `CHECKING THE SUN AGAIN.` → `A FIELD GUIDE TO THOUGHTS.`

segments.voice: The desert, here, means the Christian monks and nuns who went out into the deserts of Egypt and nearby lands to pray, later called the desert fathers and mothers. Evagrius of Pontus lived among them and wrote short, sharp sayings on the inner life. First, thoughts. Evagrius uses the Greek word logismoi, thoughts, for the patterns that pull a person away from prayer. In his work called the Praktikos he names eight: gluttony, lust, greed, sadness, anger, acedia, vainglory and pride. Second, acedia, the one in the hook. He calls it the noonday demon, the restlessness that makes the day seem endless and every other place look better. Third, watching. Evagrius advises observing the thoughts closely: when they come, how strong they are, which one follows which. Like a doctor, he studies the pattern rather than just suffering it. He understood these thoughts as the work of demons, and writes that way. Some readers outside his faith still take up the method: see it clearly, and name it. Fourth, answering. In another book he gathers short lines of scripture to say back to each thought when it arrives. Name it, then answer it. Some historians trace the later Western list of deadly sins back, through the monk John Cassian, to this desert list. That's a long road from a stone cell and a monk checking the sun.
screen: `MONKS AND NUNS IN THE DESERT.` · `LOGISMOI: THE THOUGHTS.` · `ACEDIA, THE NOONDAY DEMON.` · `WATCH IT. NAME IT. ANSWER IT.`

segments.voice: Wait for whatever shows up; it will. When a thought pulls at you, give it a plain one-word name, the way a field guide would: worry, wanting, irritation, restlessness, planning. Don't argue with it or follow it; just name it and come back to the breath, and if the same one keeps coming, that's useful information, not a failure.
The desert. The early Christian monks and nuns of Egypt and beyond, among them Evagrius, who mapped the thoughts that trouble prayer. Today's word.
Your line: name the thought. Even the noonday demon has a name. See you tomorrow.

1370.title: The Jesus Prayer
1370.hook: one short line, said over and over, moving from the lips toward the heart
1370.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians pray the Jesus Prayer, often with a knotted prayer rope, repeating it quietly through the day, and monks and others who practice hesychasm learn it under the guidance of a spiritual father or mother.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the desert, and Evagrius watching the thoughts like a doctor. Your line was name the thought. Today, a prayer that grew out of that same desert soil.

A knotted cord of black wool, looped around a wrist. Each knot is tied in a small cross. An Orthodox Christian moves a thumb from one knot to the next, and with each one says a single line, quietly: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me. On a bus. Waiting for coffee. Lying awake. Just that line, again, until it feels less like something said and more like something breathed. You met this prayer briefly on day one hundred two. Today, the tradition of stillness it lives in.
screen: `A KNOTTED CORD.` → `ONE LINE, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` → `SAID, THEN BREATHED.`

segments.voice: Hesychasm comes from the Greek hesychia, stillness. It names a way of prayer in Eastern Orthodox Christianity, kept especially by monks, and gathered in a collection of writings called the Philokalia. First, the words come from the Gospels. In Luke, a tax collector stands far off and prays, in the old King James wording, "God be merciful to me a sinner." A blind man by the road calls out, "Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me." The Jesus Prayer gathers such cries into one line; some end it with a sinner. Second, the breath. Some writers in the Philokalia describe saying the prayer with the rhythm of breathing, the first half on the in-breath, the second on the out-breath, with the attention resting low, near the heart. Third, the heart: your line. Orthodox teachers speak of the prayer moving from the lips, to the mind, to the heart, until it becomes the prayer of the heart. The heart here means the center of the whole person, not just feelings. Fourth, a caution the tradition gives itself. The breathing methods are a help, not the point, and this prayer is best learned with a spiritual father or mother, not from a book or an app. For Orthodox Christians this is not a technique for calm; it's speaking to Christ. So for anyone outside that faith, the respectful way in is to listen and learn, the way you'd sit quietly at the back of someone else's church.
screen: `HESYCHIA: STILLNESS.` · `WORDS FROM THE GOSPELS.` · `WITH THE BREATH, TOWARD THE HEART.` · `LEARNED WITH A GUIDE.`

segments.voice: If you pray as a Christian, you can say the Jesus Prayer slowly, without forcing the breath. If you don't, simply sit in the stillness the word hesychia points to, letting the breath come and go on its own. Notice where your attention rests in the body, and let it drift down toward the center of the chest.
Hesychasm. From the Greek for stillness: the Orthodox way of prayer in which the Jesus Prayer moves from the lips toward the heart. Today's word.
Your line: the prayer of the heart. The center of the whole person. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1371.title: The pilgrim
1371.hook: a wanderer hears one verse in church and sets out across Russia to learn what it means
1371.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians read The Way of a Pilgrim as an introduction to the Jesus Prayer, and some take up the prayer with a prayer rope through the day, ideally under the guidance of a spiritual father or mother.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hesychasm, the Orthodox way of stillness, and the Jesus Prayer moving from the lips toward the heart. Your line was the prayer of the heart. Today, a man who carried that prayer on foot.

A man stands in a Russian church, listening to the reading. One line from a letter of Paul catches him and won't let go. In the King James wording it's three words: "Pray without ceasing." How can anyone pray without stopping? People have to eat, sleep, work, talk. With a knapsack, some dried bread and a Bible, he starts walking, from church to church, from preacher to preacher, asking the same question. Plenty of them explain why prayer matters. Nobody tells him how.
screen: `ONE LINE IN CHURCH.` → `PRAY WITHOUT CEASING.` → `A KNAPSACK AND A QUESTION.`

segments.voice: The Way of a Pilgrim is a Russian book, written as one man's account of his own wandering. The pilgrim never gives his name. First, the question. Paul's line in First Thessalonians sounds like a slogan. The pilgrim takes it literally, and the book takes his question seriously: if it's in the Bible, there must be a way. Second, the teacher. After a long search he meets an elder, a starets, who finally answers him: the way to pray without ceasing is the Jesus Prayer, said over and over. He hands the pilgrim the Philokalia to read, and gives him a daily number of prayers to say on a prayer rope. Then he doubles it. Then doubles it again. Third, the change. At first, the pilgrim tells us, it's work. Then it gets easier. Then the prayer seems to keep going on its own, under everything, while he walks, while he talks, even while he's half asleep. He describes warmth in his heart and a new tenderness toward everyone he meets. Fourth, the road. The book is full of the people he runs into: thieves, a family who takes him in, travelers with stories of their own. The prayer doesn't pull him away from the world. It walks him into it. Some Orthodox readers come to the Jesus Prayer through this book, and the pilgrim keeps pointing back to his elder and the Philokalia. It's a picture of taking one line completely seriously.
screen: `ONE LINE TAKEN LITERALLY.` · `THE ELDER AND THE PRAYER ROPE.` · `IT STARTS TO PRAY ITSELF.` · `IT WALKS HIM INTO THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Choose one line or word to carry: if you pray, a line you already know from your own tradition, maybe yesterday's Jesus Prayer if you're a Christian; if you don't, a single plain word you'd like to live in, such as patience or here. Say it silently, again and again, at whatever pace comes naturally. When you drift, come back to it without scolding; let it grow familiar.
The pilgrim. The unnamed wanderer of The Way of a Pilgrim, who walked across Russia asking how to pray without ceasing and learned the Jesus Prayer. Today's word.
Your line: without ceasing. Under everything, like the pilgrim's prayer on the road. See you tomorrow.

1372.title: The cloud of unknowing
1372.hook: an old English guide says God can be reached by love, but never by thought
1372.howItsDone: Readers of The Cloud of Unknowing sit in silence with one short word, such as God or love, and return to it whenever thoughts arrive; the book is also a source for later Christian practices of silent prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the pilgrim, walking across Russia to learn how to pray without ceasing. Your line was without ceasing.

Stop trying to figure God out. That instruction, more or less, sits at the heart of a small English book whose writer never signed it. The book opens with a warning: whoever holds it shouldn't pass it around to the merely curious, only to someone who means to give their whole life to the practice it describes. A few chapters in, comes the instruction that sounds backwards for a book about God. Put your thinking down. Not because thinking is bad, the writer says, but because it can't reach that far. Something else can.
screen: `AN UNSIGNED BOOK, WITH A WARNING.` → `STOP TRYING TO FIGURE GOD OUT.` → `SOMETHING ELSE CAN REACH.`

segments.voice: The book is called The Cloud of Unknowing, and its picture has two layers. Above you, between you and God, hangs a cloud of unknowing: dark, thick, impossible to see through with the mind. Below you, the writer asks you to lay down a cloud of forgetting, and put under it everything else: plans, worries, even good thoughts about holy things. In chapter six an imagined student asks the obvious question: so how am I supposed to think about God? The writer's answer, in plain paraphrase: I don't know. God can be loved, but not thought. By love God can be reached and held; by thought, never. So the job isn't to clear the cloud. It's to keep knocking on it, as the book puts it, with a sharp dart of longing love, and not to walk away whatever happens. Take one short word, the writer says, a single syllable is best, like God or love. Fasten it to your heart. When thoughts crowd in, answer every one with that word. The Bible has a picture like it, at the mountain in Exodus: "And the people stood afar off, and Moses drew near unto the thick darkness where God was." Not into light. Into thick darkness. A mantra, the desert's plain names, the Jesus Prayer, the pilgrim's line: this week kept handing a busy mind something small to hold. This book's word doesn't ride the breath. It's sent upward, like a knock, whenever a thought gets in the way.
screen: `A CLOUD ABOVE, A CLOUD OF FORGETTING BELOW.` · `LOVED, BUT NOT THOUGHT.` · `A SHARP DART OF LONGING LOVE.` · `ONE WORD, FASTENED TO THE HEART.` · then, large: `MOSES DREW NEAR UNTO THE THICK DARKNESS.`

segments.voice: Choose a short word: if you pray, the book suggests God or love; if you don't, love works on its own, or any small word you care about. Don't tie it to the breath; just hold it ready. When a thought arrives, a plan, a worry, a clever idea about this practice, answer it with the word and let the thought slide under the cloud of forgetting.
The cloud of unknowing. The dark the mind can't see through, between the seeker and God, in an old English guide. Its way through is love, aimed like a dart, not thought. Today's word.
Your line: by love, not thought. A knock on the cloud, not a key to it. Until tomorrow.
